# Exercise and physical therapy in PD — concept pack

> Source-anchored research for Exercise and physical therapy in PD. Run status: COMPLETED.

## Vocabulary

- **self**: Exercise and physical therapy in PD (15/5)

## Structure and components

- [statement] SPARX3 (NCT04284436) is a phase 3 multicenter randomized evaluator-blinded treadmill endurance-exercise trial in persons with PD diagnosed within 3 years and untreated with symptomatic therapy, comparing moderate intensity (60–65% of maximum heart rate) with high intensity (80–85%) at 4 days per week and 30 minutes per session, with change in the MDS-UPDRS motor score (Part III) over 12 months as the primary outcome. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9535216/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT04284436

## Measurements and reference values

- [statement] For balance training the APTA clinical practice guideline states evidence quality high and recommendation strength strong; the Cochrane network meta-analysis reports that gait/balance/functional training probably has a moderate beneficial effect on the severity of motor signs (MD -7.50, 95% CI -11.39 to -3.48; moderate confidence; negative estimates reflect improvement); and a physiotherapy meta-analysis of 191 trials reports that balance and gait training, among other modalities, improved motor symptoms, balance, and gait. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7564288/
- [statement] For flexibility exercises the APTA clinical practice guideline states evidence quality low and recommendation strength weak, noting that the evidence quality was rated low because there was only 1 study of moderate quality that met the inclusion criteria; the Cochrane network meta-analysis reports that the evidence is very uncertain about the effect of flexibility training on the severity of motor signs (MD 4.20, 95% CI -1.61 to 9.92; very low confidence). (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/
- [statement] In the PD REHAB multicenter, open-label randomized trial in the United Kingdom (762 patients with mild to moderate PD; 381 randomized to physiotherapy and occupational therapy and 381 to no therapy), there was no difference between groups at 3 months in the primary outcome, the Nottingham Extended Activities of Daily Living score (difference 0.5 points; 95% CI -0.7 to 1.7), and the authors concluded that the evidence does not support the use of low-dose, patient-centered, goal-directed physiotherapy and occupational therapy in patients in the early stages of PD; the NIHR Health Technology Assessment report of the same trial concluded that NHS physiotherapy and occupational therapy did not produce immediate or long-term clinically meaningful improvements in ADL or quality of life. (medium confidence) — https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26785394/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5018686/

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] NICE guideline NG71 (published 19 July 2017; its overview page states last reviewed 19 December 2024) recommends offering Parkinson's disease-specific physiotherapy to people experiencing balance or motor function problems (recommendation 1.7.3) and considering referral of people in the early stages to a physiotherapist with experience of Parkinson's disease (recommendation 1.7.2); the 2024 German Society for Neurology guideline states that people with PD and impairment from motor symptoms in everyday life should have access to physiotherapy treatment. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71/chapter/Recommendations · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng71, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11157782/
- [statement] The Cochrane network meta-analysis of 154 RCTs (7837 participants, mostly mild to moderate disease) found little evidence of differences between exercise types and noted that the exact exercise type might be secondary; the earlier Cochrane physiotherapy review reported no evidence that the treatment effect differed across physiotherapy interventions (based on indirect comparisons), and the APTA guideline states that its aerobic exercise studies suggest no single form of aerobic exercise was superior to another. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/
- [statement] Sources differ in how firmly they describe exercise as slowing PD progression: the Parkinson's Foundation exercise page and a physiotherapy review state progression-related benefits (slowed symptom progression, a potential neuroprotective effect, delayed disability), whereas the APTA guideline, a review by Crotty and Schwarzschild and the SPARX3 protocol describe whether exercise modifies disease progression as an open question. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://www.parkinson.org/living-with-parkinsons/treatment/exercise · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11382789/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7318912/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9535216/
- [statement] Adverse-event statements in the sources include the following: the Cochrane network meta-analysis states that the evidence is very uncertain about the effect of physical exercise on the risk of adverse events (very low confidence), with falls (18 studies) and pain (10 studies) the most frequently reported events; the APTA guideline reports minor musculoskeletal injuries in some aerobic exercise studies, most of which resolved without incident; the SPARX phase 2 trial reported that anticipated adverse musculoskeletal events were not severe; and PD REHAB reported no difference in adverse events. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5838616/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26785394/
- [statement] Reviews state limits in trial quality: the Cochrane physiotherapy review considered the trials to be at a mixed risk of bias and said the quality of most included trials was not high; the physiotherapy meta-analysis by Radder and colleagues stated that methodological quality and reporting was highly variable and often inadequate and that most trials had relatively small sample sizes; and the Cochrane network meta-analysis reported that confidence in the effects ranged from moderate to very low, that studies were very small, and that larger, well-conducted studies are needed. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7564288/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] Reviews report improved motor-severity scores for exercise or physiotherapy versus control: the Cochrane physiotherapy review (39 trials, 1827 participants) reported a UPDRS motor difference of -5.01 points (95% CI -6.30 to -3.72); the Cochrane network meta-analysis reported mean differences of -5.76 for endurance training and -4.96 for strength/resistance training, both rated low confidence, with a stated minimum clinically important difference of -2.5; and a meta-analysis of 18 aerobic-exercise trials (901 patients) reported a standardised mean difference of -0.57 for motor actions. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4077570/
- [statement] Sources differ on whether high-intensity aerobic exercise gives greater motor benefit than moderate intensity: the SPARX phase 2 trial found that only its high-intensity treadmill arm reached a predefined nonfutility threshold, whereas a systematic review of vigorous-intensity aerobic exercise found no statistically significant differences versus moderate or low intensity and called the evidence too limited to allow recommendations for clinical practice. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5838616/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32978867/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/

## Facts and statements

- [statement] The APTA clinical practice guideline and the Cochrane network meta-analysis state different certainty ratings for aerobic (endurance) exercise and for resistance training: APTA labels both with high evidence quality and strong recommendation strength, while the Cochrane review rates confidence as low for endurance training and for strength/resistance training on the severity of motor signs. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/
- [statement] Sources differ on whether exercise or physiotherapy improved quality of life: the APTA guideline, the Cochrane network meta-analysis (low confidence for gait/balance/functional training) and a large physiotherapy meta-analysis report quality-of-life improvements for some interventions, whereas the PD REHAB trial, the earlier Cochrane physiotherapy review and a meta-analysis of aerobic exercise report no significant quality-of-life difference. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7564288/, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26785394/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/
- [statement] The trial registry record for NCT04284436 lists SPARX3 as active, not recruiting (status verified 2026-04), with enrollment 370 (actual), primary completion estimated 2027-07-31, last update posted 2026-07-10, and no results posted. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-11-27) — https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies/NCT04284436 · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
- [statement] Reviews state that follow-up evidence is limited: the Cochrane physiotherapy review found benefit in most outcomes over the short term (less than 3 months), the aerobic exercise meta-analysis reported no valid evidence on follow-up effects, the physiotherapy meta-analysis by Radder and colleagues stated that it was not possible to perform a meta-analysis on long-term effects, and the Cochrane network meta-analysis analysed effects only up to six weeks after the intervention; the APTA guideline states that gains appear to dissipate if exercise is discontinued. (high confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7120224/ · keywords: Exercise and physical therapy in PD · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4077570/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7564288/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11001292/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9046970/

## Research summary — Exercise and physical therapy in PD

Guidelines read here (NICE NG71, the APTA physical therapist guideline and the German Society for Neurology guideline) include physiotherapy statements. APTA grades aerobic exercise, resistance training and balance training as high evidence quality with strong recommendations, and flexibility exercises as low and weak. A Cochrane network meta-analysis of 154 RCTs reported benefits for most exercise types, little evidence of differences between types, and confidence from moderate to very low. Sources differ on quality-of-life effects and on high versus moderate intensity, and the PD REHAB trial found no difference in its primary outcome for physiotherapy plus occupational therapy. Reviews describe follow-up evidence as short, and sources differ on whether exercise slows progression. SPARX3, a phase 3 high-intensity treadmill trial, was listed as active, not recruiting, with no results posted.

## Source disagreement — Exercise and physical therapy in PD

Quality-of-life findings differ: APTA, the Cochrane network meta-analysis and Radder report improvements for some interventions, while PD REHAB, the earlier Cochrane review and Shu report no significant difference.

## Source disagreement — Exercise and physical therapy in PD

High versus moderate intensity: the SPARX phase 2 trial reported only its high-intensity arm reached the nonfutility threshold, while a systematic review found no statistically significant difference between vigorous and moderate or low intensity.
